facts.F12: The defendant warned the plaintiff of the intended cancellation.
facts.F13: The plaintiff had knowledge of the miscalculation.

facts.F3: The date for completion was 15th May 1973, with time being of the essence of the contract.

facts.F10: One-sixth of the total area of the premises was still occupied by the defendant's goods and machines.
facts.F11: The defendant verbally agreed with the plaintiff but did not honour it.
facts.F12: The defendant asked for a one-month extension.

Whether the de minimis rule applies to the situation.
Whether the plaintiff waived the condition that time was of the essence.
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to recover the deposit and expenses.

facts.F1: The parties are relatives living in Shui Hau Village in Lantau Island.
facts.F2: The plaintiff is the registered owner of Lot No. 372 (“Lot 372”) in Demarcation District 326 (“DD 326”).
facts.F3: The defendants are registered owners as tenants in common of Lot 365RP and Lot 371.
facts.F4: The plaintiff claims that he built a house on Lot 372 around 1980 and has put up a fence (with gates) around an area which encompassed Lot 372, Lot 365RP and Lot 371 and has been occupying these lots since without ever obtaining permission or license from the defendants or their predecessors-in-title.

facts.F8: The plaintiff negotiated with the defendants and allowed a survey to take place in 2016.

Whether the plaintiff had the requisite intention to possess (animus possidendi) for over 20 years prior to commencement of the proceedings.
Whether the alleged 1994 oral agreement between the plaintiff and the defendants’ predecessor-in-title existed.

claim: Repayment of a loan of HK$1.4 million.

facts.F2: The defendants needed funds for the deposit, mortgage, and other expenses to complete the purchase.
facts.F3: The parties were involved in a company called Willwin Development (Asia) Company Limited, which had a bank account at Standard Chartered Bank.
facts.F4: The plaintiff and the 1st defendant were the only shareholders in the company, with the plaintiff owning 70% and the 1st defendant owning 30%.
facts.F5: The plaintiff and the 1st defendant had a conversation about the mortgage details, repayment schedule, and property location.
facts.F6: The plaintiff loaned his share of the dividend, HK$1.4 million, to the defendants to help with the property purchase.

facts.F11: The defendants' version of events was inconsistent with the documentary evidence.

Whether the loan was repaid by the defendants.
Whether the defendants' version of events is credible.

facts.F1: The plaintiff is the registered owner of the premises in question, that is flat number 1901 and 1902 on the 19th floor of Sun Hing Building, No. 607, Nathan Road.
facts.F2: Wong Loon Tin, whom I shall hereinafter refer to as the 1st defendant, was the monthly tenant of flat No. 1091 and Chu Wai Peng whom I shall hereinafter refer to as the 2nd defendant, was the monthly tenant of flat No. 1902.
facts.F3: Evidence was given on behalf of the plaintiff which was not disputed that the plaintiff's solicitor in accordance with the Tenancy (Notice of Termination) Ordinance Cap. 335 served a notice to quit on the 17th day of November 1969 on both defendants.
facts.F4: On the 23rd day of December 1969 the plaintiff entered into a contract in writing on that date with one Madam Lau Sau Chun to sell the premises to Madam Lau and the contract provided for the delivery of vacant possession of the said premises in June 1970.
facts.F5: The plaintiff's solicitor sent a notice to quit to both defendants in accordance with the Tenancy (Notice of Termination) Ordinance in November 1969.
facts.F6: The defendants received notices to quit, which terminated both tenancies on the 31st May 1970.
facts.F7: The document Exh. P9 is a legally enforceable agreement in writing between the plaintiff and Madam Lau Sau Chun whereby the plaintiff agreed to sell to Madam Lau the two flats in question at a purchase price of $129,000 and vacant possession of the said premises would be delivered in June 1970.
facts.F8: The contract was entered into on the 23rd of December 1969 and therefore the provisions of the Security of Tenure (Domestic Premises) Ordinance 1970 did not apply to the premises in question.
facts.F9: The notices to quit having become effective on the 31st day of May 1970 the provisions of the Rent Increases (Domestic Premises) Control Ordinance 1970 do not apply to the premises in question.
facts.F10: The defendants refused to quit their respective premises and are now occupying them as trespassers.
facts.F11: Evidence was accepted from Mr. Lim Chong Teck, Madam Lau Sau Chun, and her brother that the contract between the plaintiff and Madam Lau Sau Chun was entered into on December 23, 1969
facts.F12: Madam Lau Sau Chun and her brother testified that the contract provided for the delivery of vacant possession of the premises in June 1970

reference_issues: Whether the plaintiff had entered into a contract to sell the premises before the coming into force of the Security of Tenure (Domestic Premises) Ordinance 1970
Whether the defendants are protected by the provisions of the Security of Tenure (Domestic Premises) Ordinance 1970 and the Rent Increases (Domestic Premises) Control Ordinance 1970

Security of Tenure (Domestic Premises) Ordinance 1970
Tenancy (Notice of Termination) Ordinance Cap. 335

claim: damages for breach of contractual duty arising from what he regards as negligence in the conduct of his affairs in dealing with certain documents relating to an assignment of land
requested_remedy: damages for breach of contractual duty arising from what he regards as negligence in the conduct of his affairs in dealing with certain documents relating to an assignment of land

facts.F1: In 1969, CHOI Man-bor assigned Apartment E on the 8th Floor, Lung Man Building, Ho Man Tin Street, Kowloon to CHAN Tat-cheong.
facts.F2: In 1972, MA Chun-man, the plaintiff, gave a power of attorney to a Mr. CHAN Yee-pong in Hong Kong concerning the premises.
facts.F3: In October 1972, the plaintiff consulted the defendant solicitors concerning the sale of the premises and the power of attorney to which the documents of title were presumably produced.
facts.F4: The assignment was put through, and the documents were signed by the attorney on behalf of Mr. CHAN Tat-cheong.
facts.F5: In September 1976, the plaintiff entered into negotiations with a lady by the name of Madam LEE Siu-bing and was advised by a firm of solicitors.
facts.F6: The discrepancy in the signatures of the documents of transfer was drawn to the attention of the plaintiff, and he went back to the defendant firm for their opinion.
facts.F7: The defendant firm's reassured the plaintiff that the title was in order, but after further investigation, they tried to get in touch with Mr. CHAN Tat-cheong in Canada.
facts.F8: A Canadian lawyer, Mr. Mark, provided an affidavit identifying the T.C. Chan who had signed the power of attorney.
facts.F9: Further correspondence ensued, and eventually, a confirmatory assignment from Mr. CHAN Tat-cheong in Canada was suggested and agreed upon.
facts.F10: A draft confirmatory deed was sent, and Mr. Mark replied, agreeing to the suggestion subject to certain qualifications.
facts.F11: The confirmatory agreement was eventually signed and certified, and the assignment was completed.
facts.F12: The plaintiff claimed damages for the delay and expenses incurred due to the discrepancy in the signatures.
facts.F13: The court considered the circumstances surrounding the discrepancy in the signatures and the steps taken by the defendant solicitors to resolve the issue.
facts.F14: The discrepancy in the signatures was patent upon the documents.
facts.F15: The discrepancy in the signatures posed a possible danger to good title and might have been made the subject of question by any later purchaser.
facts.F16: A period of about three months was reasonable for the steps that might well have been taken by any one of the various solicitors firms which had become by then concerned with the arrangements between Madam Lee and the plaintiff.

reference_issues: Whether the failure to inquire into the discrepancy in the signatures and to resolve it by effective means amounts to an act of negligence as to found an action for breach of the contractual duty to take reasonable care.

claim: The Plaintiff claimed that the provisional sale and purchase agreement which he concluded with the 2nd Defendant was not a genuine sale of the suit premises.

facts.F2: The Plaintiff had previously entered into a sale and purchase agreement with the 1st Defendant, which was registered against the suit premises at the Land Office.
facts.F3: The 2nd Defendant was an Estate Agent who agreed to sell the suit premises to one of her customers for $760,000 and find a replacement flat for the Plaintiff with a larger area at a reasonable price.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff claimed that the 2nd Defendant caused amendments to be made to the Provisional Sale & Purchase Agreement without his authority.

facts.F9: The Plaintiff had fabricated evidence concerning the alleged arrangement for the 2nd Defendant to find a replacement flat for him.

claim: The plaintiff claimed damages against the defendant for having failed to discharge its duties properly and failed to exercise a reasonable standard of care in the preparation of the conveyancing.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed damages against the defendant for having failed to discharge its duties properly and failed to exercise a reasonable standard of care in the preparation of the conveyancing.
parties: Defendant: Tsang Kwok Fun trading as Dickie Tsang & Co., Solicitors (a firm)

facts.F1: The plaintiff had its director, Fung Ting, purchase the property called Tim Yuen Villa ("Tim Yuen") in the New Territories through the defendant solicitor firm.
facts.F2: The purchase took place in 1993.
facts.F3: The defendant firm dealt with the conveyancing of the property based on the instructions provided by Fung Ting.
facts.F4: The property was described in the conveyancing documents as "新界屯門順風圍第D.D.130 Lot No.2064 E.F. 兩座物業.", which included two lots of land and the structures on them.
facts.F5: The plaintiff claimed that the defendant was negligent in failing to discover and/or inform and/or advise the plaintiff that the vendor had not produced the title deeds to part of the property, namely, Lot Nos.2064DRP, 2064GRP, and 2064RP in Demarcation District No.130.
facts.F6: Fung Ting gave evidence that he had intended to purchase the whole area of Tim Yuen as demarcated by the boundary wall erected thereon.
facts.F7: He said that he had told the defendant's staff, Chan Lap Bong, that the property concerned was inclusive of a garden wall and two 3-storey buildings.
facts.F8: Chan Lap Bong gave evidence that Fung had specified that he wanted to buy the two lots of 2064E and 2064F with the structures.
facts.F9: He also stated that he had advised Fung to engage a surveyor to prepare a report on the property, but Fung had rejected the idea.
facts.F10: Fung claimed that Chan had assured him that everything had been done properly and that the title deeds had been obtained.
facts.F11: Fung later discovered that he did not own all the lots within Tim Yuen and that his ownership extended to 2064E & F only and not the other smaller lots.
facts.F12: Madam Wong, another director of the plaintiff, confirmed that she had asked Chan whether it was necessary to get a surveyor to measure the land, but Chan had advised against it.
facts.F13: The court found that the plaintiff did not instruct the defendant to purchase the whole area of Tim Yuen as demarcated by the boundary wall erected thereon.
facts.F14: It was found that the defendant followed the instructions of the plaintiff in preparing the conveyance documents.
facts.F15: Fung Ting rejected the idea of the defendant to engage a surveyor to prepare a report on the property.
facts.F16: The plaintiff only purchased two lots of land (2064E and 2064F) with the structures on them.

reference_issues: Whether the defendant was liable for its handling of the conveyancing of the property.
What property did the vendor, Leung Tim Moon, and the plaintiff intend to sell and purchase?
What instructions were given to Chan Lap Pong of the defendant by Fung of the plaintiff?
Did the defendant breach its duty and/or act negligently as solicitors for the plaintiff in the purchase of the subject property?

claim: HK$2,592,000.00 plus interest for damages due to the Defendant's failure to complete the sale of the Property
requested_remedy: HK$2,592,000.00 plus interest for damages due to the Defendant's failure to complete the sale of the Property

facts.F1: The Plaintiff agreed to sell and the Defendant agreed to purchase the Property at the price of HK$8,380,000.00, with completion to take place on or before 23 July 2008, according to an agreement in writing dated 15 February 2008.
facts.F2: The Defendant paid deposits of HK$838,000.00 or 10% of the purchase price as required.
facts.F3: The Defendant failed to complete the sale of the Property by paying the balance of the purchase price on 23 July 2008.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff accepted the Defendant's repudiation and forfeited the deposits by letter dated 23 July 2008.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff instructed Midland Realty Ltd. to offer the Property for resale at the price of HK$7,800,000.00 on 31 July 2008, which was later reduced to HK$5,350,000.00 on 5 November 2008.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff entered into a provisional agreement to resell the Property for HK$4,950,000.00 on 27 November 2008, and the sale was completed on 20 February 2009.
facts.F7: The open market value of the Property as at 23 July 2008 was HK$7,000,000.00, as indicated by the Joint Expert Report of the parties.
facts.F8: The property prices in the New Territories were relatively stable in July and August 2008, according to the price indices.
facts.F9: The global financial crisis caused an alarming slump in the property market starting from the end of September 2008.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff did not possess the information on the open market value of the Property at the time of resale.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff was advised by estate agents when fixing the resale price of the Property.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff did not commission expert valuation before fixing the resale price of the Property.

reference_issues: Whether the Plaintiff failed to mitigate its loss by setting the resale price of the Property at HK$7,800,000.00
Whether the Plaintiff was justified in adopting a higher price than the assessed market value as a starting point for resale

claim: The plaintiff claimed damages for breach of contract, rescission of the Tenancy Agreement, and the sum of $218,162.50 which represented the total of the two payments made by the plaintiff to the defendant.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed damages for breach of contract, rescission of the Tenancy Agreement, and the sum of $218,162.50 which represented the total of the two payments made by the plaintiff to the defendant.

facts.F1: A provisional agreement for tenancy was made between the plaintiff and the defendant on 6 May 1999.
facts.F2: The tenancy agreement was for House 7, Windsor Park, Nos.2-88 Ma Ling Path, Kau To, Shatin for two years commencing on 1 June 1999 and ending on 31 May 2001 at the rent of $72,000 per month, inclusive of rates and management fee.
facts.F3: The plaintiff paid the sum of $72,000 to the defendant as the initial deposit upon signing of the Provisional Agreement.
facts.F4: A Tenancy Agreement was signed by the defendant on 21 May 1999 to confirm the terms of the Provisional Agreement.
facts.F5: The Tenancy Agreement was signed by the plaintiff on 24 May 1999.
facts.F6: The plaintiff paid to the defendant the total sum of $146,165.50 which represented the balance of the rental deposit, first month’s rent and half share of the stamp duty for the stamping of the Tenancy Agreement.
facts.F7: The defendant did not repair the water leakage of and in the premises on or before the agreed date of 26 May 1999.
facts.F8: The water leakage of and in the premises rendered the premises unfit for habitation.
facts.F9: The term of the tenancy did not commence on 1 June 1999 or at all.
facts.F10: The 3rd party commenced demolition works on House 6, which shared a common party wall with House 7, in June 1998.
facts.F11: The demolition works caused vibrations, which resulted in cracks appearing in House 7.
facts.F12: Water seepage occurred in House 7, affecting various parts of the ground floor and first floor.
facts.F13: The water seepage was caused by the penetration of water into House 7 from House 6.
facts.F14: The water seepage rendered House 7 unfit for habitation.
facts.F15: The defendant claimed against the 3rd party for indemnity and/or damages for negligence and/or nuisance.
facts.F16: The 3rd party denied the claims, stating that the water seepage was caused by internal defects in House 7 rather than the demolition works on House 6.
facts.F17: The court assessed the evidence of the two experts, Mr Hui and Mr Chan.
facts.F18: Mr. Chan's testimony was found to be more credible.
facts.F19: The court found that the water seepage was likely caused by internal defects in House 7 rather than the demolition works on House 6.

reference_issues: Whether the defendant breached the terms of the Provisional Agreement and the Tenancy Agreement by failing to repair the water leakage in the premises.
Whether the water seepage was caused by the demolition works on House 6 or internal defects in House 7.
Whether the defendant is entitled to indemnity and/or damages from the 3rd party.

claim: The difference in the purchase price of a shop premises, expenses of the resale, and licence fees and/or mesne profits from 15th February 1995
requested_remedy: The difference in the purchase price of a shop premises, expenses of the resale, and licence fees and/or mesne profits from 15th February 1995

facts.F2: The completion was agreed to be on 14 days notice, with a schedule for payment of the purchase price.
facts.F3: The Defendant failed to complete the payment on the agreed date and requested extensions of time, which were granted by the Plaintiff.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff gave formal notice to the Defendant to complete before 5 p.m. on 28th February 1995, which the Defendant failed to do.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff terminated the agreement, and the Defendant left the premises on 9th March 1995 without returning the keys.
facts.F6: The property was resold by the Plaintiff for $7500000 on 29th April 1995.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff obtained an up-to-date valuation of the property of $7300000 before the resale.
facts.F8: The Defendant opposed the Plaintiff's claim, arguing that the Plaintiff failed to mitigate the loss and that the property was sold at a price below its true value.
facts.F9: The Defendant produced a valuation report by Chung Sen Surveyors Ltd. giving the open market value of the property at $9500000.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff produced a valuation report by Richard Ellis Ltd. giving the value as $7300000.
facts.F11: The court considered the reports and evidence of the surveyors and accepted the Plaintiff's valuation as more likely to be accurate.
facts.F12: The Defendant had a potential bank loan.
facts.F13: The market was falling at the time of resale.
facts.F14: The Defendant did not hand over the keys to the premises.
facts.F15: The Plaintiff had already granted two extensions of time to the Defendant.

Whether the Plaintiff failed to mitigate the loss by not granting a further delay of 20 days as requested by the Defendant.
Whether the property was sold at a price below its true value.
Whether the Plaintiff is entitled to mesne profits for the period until vacant possession was obtained.

facts.F2: The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant breached its duty in contract and in tort, causing them to suffer various ailments and financial losses.
facts.F3: The Amended Statement of Claim included claims for damages under three sub-paragraphs: 26(a), 26(b), and 26(c).

facts.F1: The Plaintiff is the landlord of certain domestic premises in Waterloo Road of which the Defendant is the tenant.
facts.F2: The tenancy is a month to month tenancy for $500 per month.
facts.F3: On June 25th, the Plaintiff served a notice to quit on the Defendant under the provision of Section 7(2)(a) of the Rent Increases (Domestic Premises) Control Ordinance, 1970.
facts.F4: The notice to quit purported to terminate the tenancy of the Defendant on July 31st 1970.
facts.F5: The Defendant has not yielded up possession to the Plaintiff.
facts.F6: The Defendant disputes the right of the landlord to serve the notice to quit through a counter notice under Section 7(6) of the Rent Increases (Domestic Premises) Control Ordinance.
facts.F7: The parties dispute whether the counter notice was served correctly upon the Plaintiff.
facts.F8: The Plaintiff made an application to the Supreme Court for an order for possession.
facts.F9: The Supreme Court judge ordered the transfer of the case to the District Court under section 11 of the District Court (Civil Jurisdiction and Procedure) Ordinance (Cap. 336).
facts.F10: The case would have had to be tried twice if proceedings in the Supreme Court had continued without a decision on whether a counter-notice was served.
facts.F11: Proceedings would take place in the Supreme Court first if it hadn't been transferred to the District Court.

lawsuit_type: Action for the recovery of possession of a domestic premises
reference_issues: Whether a counter notice was served correctly upon the Plaintiff under Section 7(6) of the Rent Increases (Domestic Premises) Control Ordinance.
Whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear the case given the exclusive jurisdiction of the District Court under Section 7(7) of the Ordinance.

facts.F1: The registered owner of 81 Nathan Road, ground floor, was Mr. Harilela.
facts.F2: In 1966, the premises were let to one Pang Liu on 1st May for a term of 3 years.
facts.F3: Pang Liu defaulted in payment of his rent, leading to Mr. Harilela re-entering as against Pang Liu.
facts.F4: Kwan Kau agreed to take over the principal tenancy subject to existing sub-tenancies.
facts.F5: By lease dated 29th December 1966, the premises were let to Kwan Kau for a period of 2 years and 5 months commencing from 1st December 1966.
facts.F6: Kwan Kau sublet a portion of the premises to each of the defendants in the five actions.
facts.F7: On 15th June 1968, Mr. Harilela re-entered upon the whole of the ground floor in exercise of his powers under clause 5(a) of the lease.
facts.F8: On 17th June 1968, Mr. Harilela wrote to each of the defendants informing them that their sub-tenancies with Kwan Kau had come to an end, and offering them tenancies for the remaining term of the lease (10 months) at the same rent.
facts.F9: The defendants accepted the offer in writing.
facts.F10: Early in May 1969, the plaintiff closed the entrances to the arcade, preventing the three stall-holders from doing any business.
facts.F11: On 16th May, the three stall-holders applied to Mr. Justice McMullin for a mandatory order that the plaintiff open the entrances to the arcade to enable them to do business, which was refused.
facts.F12: The plaintiff applied for summary judgment in each case under O.27 r.3.
facts.F13: The defendants applied to amend their pleadings based on advice from their counsel.
facts.F14: The 1962 Ordinance requires a notice of termination period, the defendants received a 10 months' notice, which was more than the required period.
facts.F15: The 10 months period given to the defendants ended in April 1969.

reference_issues: Whether the letter from Mr. Harilela to the defendants on 17th June 1968 was capable of being construed as a 10 months' notice to quit.

requested_remedy: Damages under the heads of loss of rental income and damages for discomfort, distress, and inconvenience
parties: Plaintiff: Gwong Leung Property Holdings Limited

facts.F1: The plaintiff commenced the present proceedings against the defendant on 11 November 2016.
facts.F2: The action is based on negligence, trespass and/or nuisance, and the rule under Rylands v Fletcher.
facts.F3: The plaintiff obtained an interlocutory judgment against the defendant with damages to be assessed, as well as an injunction restraining the defendant from causing any water leakage from the defendant’s property to the plaintiff’s property.
facts.F4: The defendant is the registered owner of the flat situated on the 2nd floor of the same building as the plaintiff’s property.
facts.F5: The plaintiff’s property was divided into six rooms, and the present litigation concerned one of them, which was identified as Room F.
facts.F6: Room F was not located exactly under the defendant’s property.
facts.F7: In or about early February 2016, the tenant complained to the plaintiff about the water seepage problem.
facts.F8: The tenant of Room F terminated the tenancy prematurely, and moved out of Room F at the end of February 2016.
facts.F9: The plaintiff was not able to rent out the room again.
facts.F10: The plaintiff sold the property to a third party in October 2017 (and the transaction was completed in November 2017).
facts.F11: The expert report adduced by the plaintiff indicated that, due to the water seepage problem, there were spots of debonded plastering in Room F, and that the condition of the bedroom was particularly severe.
facts.F12: The photographs taken by the expert upon the inspection on 26 August 2016 clearly show that Room F was in devastated conditions at the material times.
facts.F13: The court found that the plaintiff would not be able to lease the room out unless some remedial works were to be carried out by the defendant in his property.
facts.F14: The court disallowed the plaintiff’s interests for a period of 2 ½ years, between 11 November 2016 and 10 May 2019.

lawsuit_type: Assessment of damages in a civil action
reference_issues: Whether the plaintiff is entitled to claim loss of rental income and damages for discomfort, distress, and inconvenience

claim: The Plaintiff disputed the quantum of damages and claimed that the Defendant had already elected for common law damages only.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff disputed the quantum of damages and claimed that the Defendant had already elected for common law damages only.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff purchased a flat from the Defendant under a Sale and Purchase Agreement dated 12th June 1997 at the price of $9,287,600.00.
facts.F2: Clause 16 of the Agreement for sale and purchase provided that if the purchaser fails to observe or comply with any of the terms and conditions, the vendor may give to the purchaser notice in writing calling upon the purchaser to make good his default.
facts.F3: By a letter dated 4th June 1998, the Plaintiff purchaser alleged a breach by the Defendant vendor of the terms of the agreement and demanded the return of the deposit and part payments.
facts.F4: A writ was duly issued on 23rd June 1998.
facts.F5: By a letter dated 26th September 1998, the Defendant gave notice determining the agreement.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff had paid the 10% deposit and had also made part payments of more than $1.85m
facts.F7: On 30th September 1998, the Defendant amended its Defence and Counterclaim to claim firstly, a declaration that the Defendant is entitled to forfeit the deposit and also damages for breach of agreement.
facts.F8: On 4th November 1998, the Defendant resold the property for $4,839,400.00 incurring resale expenses of $99,208.00.
facts.F9: On 23rd March 1999, Master Jones gave final judgment for the Defendant for the declaratory relief that it was entitled to forfeit the deposit, and entered interlocutory judgment for damages for breach of the agreement to be assessed.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff’s Amended Statement of Claim was struck out.
facts.F11: On 19th April 1999, the Defendant issued the present summons for 1) interim payment of $2,689,888.20 or such other sum as the Court shall think fit by way of interim payment on account of the damages as adjudged to be assessed under the order of Master Jones, and 2) security for costs in the amount of $1,666,718.00 or such sum to the satisfaction of the Court.
facts.F12: A notice to make good the default had been given to the Plaintiff under clause 16(1), and 21 days had been allowed to elapse before the letter of 26th September.
facts.F13: The letter of 26th September permitted the Defendant to submit that it was a determination under clause 16.
facts.F14: A period of about 1 month lapsed between 26th September and 4th November.
facts.F15: There is no evidence before the court that the market had suffered a huge drop between late September and late October or early November that the price received on an actual resale did not reflect more or less the market price in late September.

reference_issues: Whether the Defendant had properly determined the agreement under clause 16 of the Sale and Purchase Agreement.
Whether the Defendant was entitled to claim damages for breach of agreement under common law or under clause 16 of the Sale and Purchase Agreement.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff commenced this action on 4 June 1999 against the 2 Defendants.

facts.F8: The court found that Madam Leung had prepared most of the documents for the present proceedings and had dictated the plaintiff's oral submissions.
facts.F9: Madam Leung had circumvented the RAOs and RPOs made against her through the present proceedings initiated by the plaintiff.

claim: claims for damages for repudiation of the tenancy agreement
requested_remedy: claims for damages for repudiation of the tenancy agreement

facts.F1: The Defendant took up a 3-year-tenancy to operate from 8th July 1993 to 7th July 1996 to lease Shop Unit 2011 for $30,000.00 per month plus other charges.
facts.F2: The Defendant spent $200,000.00 to decorate Shop Unit 2011 over 20 days and took up the tenancy to sell clothes therefrom sometime in July 1993.
facts.F3: The Defendant found that neither 80% nor 70% of Park Lane Square had been let out to prospective tenants as claimed by Jones, Lang & Wootton in their advertising brochure.
facts.F4: The shop tenants, including the Defendant, complained about not being told the truth about the occupancy rate and aired their grievances in the local press.
facts.F5: The landlord agreed to reduce rent by 30% from July to September 1993 to tenants who had paid up all outstanding rent but refused to extend the rent discount period.
facts.F6: The Defendant became aware that the landlord had decided to demolish Phase I of Park Lane Square and had served eviction notices on all tenants in Phase I giving them 6 months to leave.
facts.F7: The demolition of Phase I resulted in a substantial change in the share holding of the Plaintiff and cut off public access for shoppers from and to Nathan Road, limiting access to the entrance from Kimberley Road.
facts.F8: The Defendant surrendered possession of Shop Unit 2011 on 27th January 1994 and made part payment of the judgment debt.
facts.F9: Access and egress to Nathan Road was cut off to tenants and customers of shop units in Phase II of Park Lane Square on 30th June 1994 when the demolition of Phase I commenced.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff could have reduced the rent significantly to attract retail tenancy interest in Park Lane Square.
facts.F11: The Defendant is liable for rent and other charges from 1st February 1994 until 30th June 1994.

reference_issues: Whether the Plaintiff had taken reasonable steps to mitigate his loss in the attempts made to relet Shop Unit 2011

Whether the Plaintiff's decision to demolish Phase I of Park Lane Square at a late stage was a novus actus interveniens to deprive the Plaintiff from further damages from the vacating tenants of Phase II as damages which are too remote and thus unrecoverable

facts.F10: The 1st Defendant relied on five grounds for striking out the Plaintiffs' Statement of Claim.
facts.F11: The GCS and SCS established a sequence of procedures for finalising the sale.
